small modular reactors: Small modular reactors (SMRs) are nuclear fission reactors with electrical output of 300 MWe or less, factory-built and shipped to site. Designs include light-water (NuScale, Holtec), high-temperature gas-cooled (X-energy), and molten-salt variants. Key claimed advantages: lower upfront capital, passive safety, siting flexibility, load-following capability. As of 2024, the only SMR generating power at scale was Russia's Akademik Lomonosov; NuScale received US NRC design certification in 2023 but its first US deployment (UAMPS) was cancelled the same year due to cost overruns. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_modular_reactor
quantum error correction: Quantum error correction (QEC) protects fragile quantum information by encoding a logical qubit redundantly across many physical qubits. Foundational codes include the 9-qubit Shor code (1995), the surface code (Kitaev 1997), and the color code. Modern fault-tolerant proposals favor surface codes for their high threshold (~1%) and 2D nearest-neighbor connectivity. In 2023–2024 Google demonstrated below-threshold scaling of the surface code on the Willow chip; QuEra and IBM published work on transversal-gate logical operations. The fault-tolerance threshold theorem (Aharonov-Ben-Or, Kitaev) underpins the field. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_error_correction
superconductors: Superconductors are materials that conduct electricity with zero resistance below a critical temperature (Tc). Discovered in mercury at 4.2 K by Onnes (1911). BCS theory (1957) explained conventional superconductivity via Cooper pairs. High-Tc cuprates (YBCO, Tc ~93 K) discovered 1986 by Bednorz and Müller. Iron-based superconductors followed in 2008. The 2020s saw claims around hydrogen-rich materials at high pressure (LK-99 in 2023 was widely refuted). Applications: MRI magnets, MAGLEV trains, particle accelerators, SQUID magnetometers, and prospective fusion reactor magnets. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superconductivity
